planting.note: Move potted bulbs outdoors to shaded, humid positions only once nights stay reliably above 55F.

directions: This evergreen Brazilian forest bulb keeps its broad, often patterned leaves year-round and should never be allowed to dry out completely or drop below roughly 55F. It produces umbels of violet-blue, amaryllis-like flowers from a modest bulb that prefers a loose, humus-rich mix with excellent drainage. Grow it in filtered light under canopy or shade cloth, as direct sun scorches the foliage. It is slow to multiply, making it a true specialist collector plant rather than a mass-market bulb.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Best treated as a container plant that spends the warm season outdoors in shade and winters indoors above 55F.

directions: A classic Brazilian understory amaryllid, this species produces rounded clusters of fragrant, hyacinth-like blue to violet flowers above glossy strap leaves. It is evergreen and resents being dried out at the root for extended periods, so steady moisture and a free-draining, organic-rich substrate suit it best. Bright, filtered forest-floor light mimics its native habitat more closely than full sun. Because seedlings and offsets take years to reach flowering size, it remains a slow, patience-rewarding plant in specialist collections.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Only set the bulb's neck and upper roots in a steep, fast-draining crevice mix once warm, humid weather is settled.

directions: Famous among bulb collectors as the Empress of Brazil, this species clings to vertical granite cliff faces in its native Organ Mountains, rooting into crevices rather than soil. Cultivation mimics that habitat with an extremely sharp, mineral-heavy, almost soil-free mix kept barely moist and never waterlogged, plus high humidity around the foliage. Its fan of long, curved, sword-like leaves can take a decade or more to reach flowering size, after which it sends up tall stalks topped with large lavender-blue trumpets. Because of its demanding culture and slow growth, it is grown almost exclusively by dedicated amaryllid specialists.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant bulbs after soil has warmed following last frost, since growth and flowering both follow the arrival of warm weather.

directions: Native to dry Andean slopes of Peru and Bolivia, this small bulb produces narrow gray-green leaves and sweetly fragrant, upward-facing yellow trumpet flowers in the warm months. It grows actively in spring and summer, then wants a distinctly dry, dormant rest once foliage yellows in autumn, making a free-draining soil essential to avoid bulb rot. In frost-free climates it can be left in the ground, while in colder zones it is typically grown in pots and overwintered dry and protected. Its scent is notably strong for such a modest-sized flower, which is part of its appeal to bulb specialists.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow year-round in a shaded, humid spot and only move containers outdoors once nights stay well above 50F.

directions: This Andean cloud-forest amaryllid grows as an evergreen clumping bulb with broad, leathery leaves and never undergoes a true dry dormancy in cultivation. It produces large, waxy, intensely fragrant white flowers with a greenish throat, often compared in scent and form to Eucharis. Consistent moisture, high humidity, and a rich but well-drained, organic potting mix best replicate its misty montane habitat. It is slow to establish and multiply, so most plants in cultivation trace back to a relatively small pool of specialist-collected stock.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Set bulbs out after frost danger passes and reduce watering sharply once foliage begins to die back for its rest period.

directions: Known in the bulb trade as a queen lily, this Central American and Andean cloud-forest species produces arching stems of pendant, tubular flowers that are scarlet to coral at the base and tipped green. Its broad leaves emerge during the growing season and the bulb typically wants a drier, cooler rest once they fade. A well-drained, humus-rich mix with dappled light suits it better than full sun, reflecting its native montane forest-edge habitat. It remains uncommon outside specialist Amaryllidaceae collections due to limited propagation stock.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant after last frost and withhold water once leaves yellow, giving the bulb a dry rest through its dormant season.

directions: This Andean grassland and scrub bulb sends up narrow leaves followed by clusters of pendant, tubular orange-red flowers on a leafless stalk, a classic amaryllid display habit. It follows a seasonal growth-and-rest cycle, needing regular moisture while in leaf and a distinctly drier spell once the foliage dies back. Sharp drainage is important year-round since the bulb is prone to rot if kept wet during its rest. It is grown mainly by Andean-bulb specialists and is still only occasionally offered through specialist seed and bulb exchanges.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
